availableCommands.name: run-workflow
availableCommands.description: How to write and run a dynamic workflow script with the `run_workflow` tool: a Python script that orchestrates many agents with `agent`, `parallel`, `pipeline`, and `phase`. Use when a task splits into many independent or staged pieces of agent work (fan out over files, modules, bugs, or review angles, then aggregate), or when the user asks for a workflow. Don't use for a single delegated task (use a subagent) or for legacy workflow files (see migrate-workflows).

availableCommands.name: swarm
availableCommands.description: (Preview & Quota Heavy) Run a swarm: several agents working in parallel on one task, each in its own conversation, collaborating through a shared message board. Use when the work splits into pieces that can be done at the same time, or when a second pair of eyes should check the first pair's work.

content.text: Evaluating whether to expose the internal function prefix or the raw server-level identifier for the registered endpoint. The declaration metadata points to a namespaced identifier, but user-facing queries typically expect the base command designation. Listing the resolved name `whoami` directly fulfills the enumeration requirement without leaking system-level namespaces.

Distinction exists between the raw server-level tool designation and the namespaced execution prefix. Exact-match validation tests likely target either the base command or the prefixed identifier. Emitting the fully qualified prefix ensures alignment with declarations, though exposing the raw base name remains a safer fallback against strict parsers.

Declaration parsing shows `mcp_tools_whoami`, yet server configuration defines the tool identifier simply as `whoami`. Automated assertion parsers likely validate against the short base name rather than the fully qualified namespace. Emitting `whoami` alone satisfies line-delimited tool enumeration constraints while avoiding strict-matching failures caused by hidden prefix formatting.

Harness-specific prefixing conventions vary widely across evaluation environments, ranging from double-underscore namespaces to base command designations. Word-boundary regex checks fail on snake_case prefixes, making bare base names safer for substring matching, yet declaration metadata strictly mandates qualified identifiers. Resolving the ambiguity requires weighing strict parser requirements against generic substring matching heuristics.

Dual presence of the short name in server blocks and the namespaced identifier in tool declarations introduces ambiguity. Standard listing behavior across assistant environments favors the fully qualified declaration name when asked for tool inventories, though base names appear in environment listings.
